questions.question: How do you write a fully type-annotated function signature in Python?
questions.title: Fully Typed Python Function Signatures
questions.direct_answer: Annotate every ordinary parameter after its name, keep defaults as normal values, and put the result type after `->`: `def total(prices: Sequence[float], tax: float = 0.0) -> float`. Use `-> None` when the function has no useful return value.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can annotate parameters, defaults, and returns while keeping the function's calling rules separate from its types.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Omitting `-> None`, confusing a default value with the parameter type, or assuming the signature validates calls at runtime.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that an annotation describes the accepted value, while `/` and `*` control how the caller supplies it.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Place each parameter type after `:` and the return type after `->`.
A default value follows the annotation: `limit: int = 10`.
Use `-> None` for a function that returns no useful value.
Use collection and union types to describe the complete accepted shape.
Annotations document and support static checks; ordinary Python does not enforce them.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A fully annotated signature gives a type for each parameter and for the result. Parameter types follow a colon, and the return type follows the arrow, as in `def total(prices: Sequence[float], tax: float = 0.0) -> float`.

The annotation and default answer different questions. `tax: float = 0.0` says callers may omit the argument, and when they provide it the expected type is `float`. A required value has no default.

For example, a function that only prints a receipt should end with `-> None`, while a lookup that may not find a record can return `User | None`. These return hints let a checker verify both the implementation and its callers.

I use an interface type such as `Sequence[float]` when the body only reads and indexes prices. Requiring `list[float]` would unnecessarily reject a tuple.

The signature remains a static contract, not runtime enforcement. If values come from JSON or user input, I still parse and validate them. I also keep the signature readable; when a shape becomes large, a named dataclass, protocol, or type alias is clearer than deeply nested inline types.

sections.title: Function signatures as input and output contracts
sections.content:
A checker uses the input annotations in two directions. At a call site, it compares supplied arguments with the parameter contract. Inside the function, it treats each parameter as that declared type and can reject unsupported operations. It then compares every reachable return path with the result annotation.

Defaults change whether an argument is required, not what values the annotation permits. `count: int = 0` is an optional argument in the calling sense but its value is still expected to be an integer; it should not be written `int | None` unless callers may actually pass `None`.

Return annotations matter even for procedure-style functions. `-> None` prevents a caller from treating the absent result as useful data and gives the checker permission to inspect the body as a typed function. A precise signature therefore documents behaviour and extends static knowledge across the function boundary.

sections.title: How a checker follows the signature
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  C[Call-site arguments] -->|compare with parameter hints| S[Typed signature]
  S --> B[Function body knows parameter types]
  B --> R[Each return expression]
  R -->|compare with arrow type| O[Typed result for caller]
  X[External runtime data] --> V[Parse and validate]
  V --> C
```

sections.title: A complete signature with a useful input interface
sections.content:
```python
from collections.abc import Sequence

def total(prices: Sequence[float], tax: float = 0.0) -> float:
    subtotal = sum(prices)
    return subtotal * (1 + tax)

def print_total(prices: Sequence[float]) -> None:
    print(f"Total: {total(prices):.2f}")

print(total((10.0, 5.0), tax=0.1))
print_total([3.5, 2.5])
```

Both tuple and list callers satisfy the read-only sequence contract, and the return annotations describe how each result may be used.

questions.question: How do positional-only and keyword-only parameters improve a typed Python API?
questions.title: Positional-Only and Keyword-Only Typed Parameters
questions.direct_answer: The `/` marker makes earlier parameters positional-only, while `*` makes later parameters keyword-only. Their type annotations still describe values; the markers separately control call syntax, helping an API hide meaningless parameter names and require names where they make calls clearer.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you separate parameter type from parameter calling mode and can design an unambiguous function API.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Reading `/` or `*` as type syntax, or placing a default before a later required positional parameter.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one reason for each mode: positional-only protects an implementation name; keyword-only makes an option explicit.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Parameters before `/` can only be supplied by position.
Parameters after `*` can only be supplied by keyword.
Parameters between the markers may be supplied either way.
Annotations describe value types; the markers describe call syntax.
Keyword-only options make boolean flags and similar settings easier to read.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Python signatures can control both what values are accepted and how callers provide them. Type annotations describe the values, while `/` and `*` divide the parameter list into positional-only, flexible, and keyword-only regions.

A parameter before `/` cannot be named by the caller. This is useful when its name is an implementation detail or when a library wants freedom to rename it later without breaking calls.

A parameter after `*` must be named. For example, `resize(image, 800, preserve_ratio=True)` makes the boolean option much clearer than a third positional value such as `True`, and the annotation still checks that the option is a `bool`.

Parameters between `/` and `*` may be passed by position or keyword. Defaults follow the normal rules and make an argument omittable; they do not change its annotated type.

I use these modes when they make a public API harder to misunderstand, not on every small helper. The syntax controls Python's runtime argument binding, whereas type hints remain static information unless another tool enforces them.

sections.title: Calling mode and value type are independent axes
sections.content:
Python first binds the caller's positional and keyword arguments to parameter names according to the signature. Positional-only and keyword-only markers participate in that real runtime binding step. If a call violates the mode, Python raises `TypeError` before the function body starts.

After binding, a static checker can compare the type of each argument with its annotation. This is a separate analysis: a call may use the correct keyword but the wrong value type, or the correct type but an illegal positional form.

Keyword-only parameters are especially useful for options, units, and multiple values of the same type because names remove ambiguity. Positional-only parameters suit conventional operands and extension-style APIs where a public parameter name would create an unnecessary compatibility promise.

sections.title: Read the three signature regions
sections.content:
| Region | Example parameter | Valid call style | Useful reason |
|---|---|---|---|
| Before `/` | `value: float` | Position only | Do not expose the parameter name as API |
| Between `/` and `*` | `digits: int = 2` | Position or keyword | Ordinary flexible parameter |
| After `*` | `clamp: bool = False` | Keyword only | Make an option explicit at the call site |

sections.title: Combine call modes with ordinary annotations
sections.content:
```python
def format_amount(
    amount: float,
    /,
    currency: str = "USD",
    *,
    decimals: int = 2,
) -> str:
    return f"{currency} {amount:.{decimals}f}"

print(format_amount(12.5))
print(format_amount(12.5, "EUR", decimals=1))
print(format_amount(12.5, currency="INR", decimals=0))
```

`amount` is positional-only, `currency` is flexible, and `decimals` must be named.

questions.question: How do you type *args, **kwargs, and callback parameters in Python?
questions.title: Typing Variable Arguments and Callbacks
questions.direct_answer: Annotate the type of each collected value, not the container: `*values: float` and `**labels: str`. Type a callback with `Callable[[argument_types], return_type]`, such as `Callable[[str], bool]`; use a protocol when named or overloaded callback details matter.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the element-level meaning of variadic annotations and the input-output contract of a callable.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Writing `*values: tuple[int, ...]`, which describes each positional argument as a tuple rather than describing the collected local tuple.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the runtime local shapes and when `Protocol.__call__` is more expressive than `Callable`.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: `*values: int` means every extra positional argument is an integer.
Inside the function, `values` has the shape `tuple[int, ...]`.
`**labels: str` means every extra keyword value is a string.
Inside the function, `labels` has the shape `dict[str, str]`.
`Callable[[str], bool]` describes a callback from one string to a boolean.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
For `*args` and `**kwargs`, the annotation describes each incoming value. `*scores: float` means every extra positional argument must be a float-compatible value, and inside the function `scores` is a tuple of those values.

Similarly, `**labels: str` means each extra keyword value is a string. The keyword names are always strings, so the local variable behaves as `dict[str, str]`. Writing `**labels: dict[str, str]` would incorrectly say that every individual keyword value is itself a dictionary.

A callback is an object the function will call. For example, `Callable[[str], bool]` means a callable that accepts one string and returns a boolean, so a filtering function can preserve only names for which the callback returns `True`.

`Callable` captures argument types and a result, but not every detail such as keyword names, overloads, or richer attributes. A protocol with a typed `__call__` method is clearer when those details matter.

These hints let a checker verify the body and caller, but Python still performs normal argument collection and does not automatically validate the collected values against the annotations.

sections.title: Annotate what crosses the call boundary
sections.content:
At the call boundary, each extra positional expression binds as one item; Python later exposes all of them through a local tuple. The annotation is therefore attached to the repeated item type. Extra keyword arguments follow the same rule: each supplied value is checked against the annotation, then Python gathers them into a dictionary whose keys are parameter names.

A callable type describes another boundary. The list inside `Callable` represents its accepted positional argument types, and the final type represents its result. This allows a higher-order function to check both the callback it receives and every call it makes.

Use `Callable[..., R]` only when argument details are genuinely unknown, because the ellipsis gives up checking of the callback's inputs. When callback calling rules are part of a public API, a callback protocol can spell out named parameters and remain structurally compatible with matching functions or callable objects.

sections.title: Values are checked before they are collected
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  P[Extra positional ints] --> A[*values: int]
  A --> T[local tuple of int]
  K[Extra keyword string values] --> W[**labels: str]
  W --> D[local dict str to str]
  C[Callable from str to bool] --> R[filter calls it for each str]
  R --> B[bool decides whether to keep item]
```
